title: The hypertrophy series: using volume to assess recovery abilities
summary: He explains how to estimate your maximum recoverable volume. On paper, a good program should let you predict progress, so missing the projected numbers flags a volume problem. In the gym, getting fewer reps with the same weight signals poor recovery. Combining both turns plateaus into simple programming problems of too much or too little volume.
claims: Maximum recoverable volume is the amount of work that reaches the highest level of muscle fibre damage you can still recover and grow from
Constantly doing too little leads to stalls and plateaus, constantly doing too much leads to injury or regression
Listening to your body is too abstract; use your program and your expected rate of progression to judge recovery
His program is set up so he can predict roughly what he will deadlift two months from now; missing that projection means volume was too low or too high
If you get fewer reps with the same weight (e.g. 225 lb squats) next session, you regressed, meaning the damage created was either too little or too much
A session in between can cannibalise recovery from a lift, e.g. heavy deadlifts hurting heavy squats; play detective to find the culprit
Feeling fresh, tired or sore does not reliably tell you whether you are recovered
With warm-ups, form and the day's programming controlled, you should hit the progression written on paper; if not, either the execution or the program needs fixing
In bodybuilding a plateau is just a failure to recover from too much volume or a lack of stimulus from too little; treat it as a programming issue and manipulate volume and intensity
